teaser: Umbrellas everywhere, wet stones underfoot, and not a single raindrop in the air.
review_notes:
Dimensions 212.2 x 276.2 cm: check.
Site identified as today's Place de Dublin, near the Gare Saint-Lazare: check.
Caillebotte helping to organize and finance the 1877 Impressionist exhibition: check.
Provenance: stayed in the family until the 1950s, bought by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1964: check.
Bequest of about 68 works to the French state, only part accepted: check numbers.
Family fortune from supplying bedding to the army; brother Martial as photographer: check.
Woman's earring described as a pearl; her face seen through a dotted veil: visible in image, interpretation.

lesson.text: It is raining in this painting. The title says so, and everybody carries an umbrella. Yet search the air between the buildings: there is not one drop, not one streak. Gustave Caillebotte painted a downpour without painting any rain.
So how do you know it is wet? The evidence is all indirect, like clues at a scene. He lets the stones, the silk and the sky testify, and each one tells you the same thing in its own way.

lesson.title: Proof of rain
lesson.text: Three witnesses, and none of them is a raindrop.

spots.title: The paving stones
spots.text: Each cobble has a pale highlight on its rounded top and a dark joint around it. Dry stone is dull. Only water makes it shine like this.

spots.title: The reflections
spots.text: Under the walking man's feet, his dark legs smear down into the pavement. The street has become a faint mirror.

spots.title: The umbrella
spots.text: The stretched silk gleams silver-grey, lightest along the top where the wet cloth catches the sky.

spots.title: The sky
spots.text: No clouds are drawn, no sun either. A flat, yellowish-grey veil lights everything evenly, so there are almost no cast shadows.

lesson.text: This is a painter who trusts you to do some of the work. He gives the effects and lets your mind add the cause. Once you see that, another strange thing appears: for a picture of bad weather and a busy crossroads, it is extraordinarily calm and orderly.

The canvas is enormous: about 2.1 meters high and 2.8 meters wide (roughly 7 by 9 feet). The couple in the foreground are close to life-size. Standing before it in Chicago, you feel you are about to step aside to let them pass.

Caillebotte was 28 and had been trained with rigor. He loved perspective, the system of lines that makes a flat surface look deep. Before touching the big canvas he worked out the scene in drawings and oil sketches. The result is a street built like a piece of architecture.
The hidden framework of the picture.

lines.label: The lamp post
lines.text: The green lamp post cuts the canvas into two halves. Left: open space and small, distant walkers. Right: big figures pressed up close.

lines.label: Eye level
lines.text: Nearly every head, near or far, sits on the same horizontal line. That is the painter's eye level, and it means he stood on the pavement like any passerby.

lines.label: The wedge
lines.text: The corner building comes at us like the prow of a ship. Its two sides slide away down two different streets.

lines.label: The curb
lines.text: The edge of the sidewalk runs up from the bottom of the canvas to the foot of the lamp post, pulling you into the scene.

lesson.text: A cross in the middle, a wedge on the left, and at the right edge something no academic painter would have allowed: a man sliced in half by the frame. Critics of the time compared such cropping to photography. Caillebotte's brother Martial was a keen photographer, and Gustave thought about pictures the way a camera sees.
The scene looks like a snapshot, but nothing in it is accidental. Caillebotte gave a fleeting moment the solid construction of a classical painting.

The place itself was brand new. Under Napoleon III, the official Baron Haussmann had torn down much of medieval Paris and replaced it with wide, straight avenues lined with matching stone buildings. This crossroads, near the Saint-Lazare train station, had not existed a generation earlier.

Caillebotte grew up a few streets from this spot. His family had become rich partly by supplying bedding to the French army, and the Caillebottes lived in one of the new stone houses of this rebuilt quarter.

Not everyone found this modern city warm. Watch how the walkers move: each alone or in a pair, each under a private roof of silk, none speaking to another. Even among the pedestrians there is one traveler who stands apart from all the others.
Everyone here goes on foot, except one. Somewhere in the crowd there is a horse. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The horse
spots.text: A brown horse pulling a cab, half hidden behind the walker's umbrella. In 1877 horses were Paris's engines, yet Caillebotte reduces this one to a small note in the distance.

lesson.text: The foreground couple are the opposite: huge, sharp, impossible to miss. They are dressed in the latest fashion, he in a top hat and open overcoat, she in a fur-trimmed dress. And they are both looking at something to the left that we will never see.
The street is full of small things painted with care, and the image is detailed enough to reward wandering. Start with the couple and work your way back into the mist.

spots.title: His face
spots.text: Moustache, pale skin, eyes turned sideways. His expression is hard to pin down: curious, distracted, perhaps a little bored.

spots.title: The earring
spots.text: A single bright dot at her ear, probably a pearl. Her face is seen through a fine dotted veil.

spots.title: The cut-off man
spots.text: Only half of him fits in the picture. He is about to collide with the couple, and someone will have to tilt an umbrella.

spots.title: The cab wheel
spots.text: A red-orange wheel, the one hot color on the left side. The carriage it belongs to is slipping out of the frame.

spots.title: The walker
spots.text: Head down, hand in pocket, mid-stride. He crosses the open square alone, reflected in the wet stones.

spots.title: The far crowd
spots.text: Behind the lamp post, tiny figures thin out into blue-grey mist. Distant things are paler and blurrier, as they are in damp air.

spots.title: Matching umbrellas
spots.text: Every umbrella in the painting is the same grey. They repeat across the canvas like a pattern, one more sign of a standardized modern city.

lesson.text: Caillebotte showed the painting at the third Impressionist exhibition, in 1877, a show he helped to organize and pay for. It hung near Monet's smoky views of the Saint-Lazare station. His smooth, precise finish looked nothing like his friends' loose brushwork, and people did not quite know where to place him.

For decades he was remembered mainly as a patron. He bought his friends' unsold canvases and, when he died in 1894 at 45, left some 68 of them to the French state, which hesitated to accept them all. His own paintings stayed mostly with his family.

This one was no exception. It remained in the family until the 1950s, and the Art Institute of Chicago bought it in 1964. Only then did a wide public discover that the generous collector had also been one of the sharpest eyes of his generation.

Return to the contradiction you started with. A rainy day without rain, a crowd without contact, a snapshot built with a ruler. Caillebotte's Paris is brand new and gleaming, and everyone in it is a little alone.

quiz.question: What is missing from this painting of a rainy day?
quiz.explanation: The rain is shown only through its effects.

quiz.question: What divides the canvas into two halves?
quiz.explanation: The lamp post runs down the center of the composition.

quiz.question: Roughly how large is the painting?
quiz.explanation: The foreground figures are close to life-size.

quiz.question: Who redesigned Paris with the wide avenues seen here?
quiz.explanation: Haussmann rebuilt the city under Napoleon III.

quiz.question: What happens to the man at the right edge?
options: He is cut in half by the frame
He is looking straight at us
quiz.explanation: The cropping reminded critics of photography.

quiz.question: Which museum bought the painting in 1964?
quiz.explanation: It stayed in Caillebotte's family until the 1950s, then went to Chicago.

facts.text: Caillebotte painted long streaks of rain falling across the sky.
facts.explanation: There are no raindrops at all; shiny stones and umbrellas do the job.

facts.text: Almost all the heads in the picture sit on the same horizontal line.
facts.explanation: That line is the painter's eye level as a pedestrian.

facts.text: Caillebotte was a poor artist who depended on selling his pictures.
facts.explanation: He was wealthy and bought the unsold work of his friends.
